"The Indispensable Liberty"

A Speech Advocating Free Speech Absolutism

Prefatory Note

This represents a sincere, well-developed version of free speech absolutism - a serious intellectual tradition held by thinkers from Mill to Dworkin to many civil libertarians. I'm presenting the strongest honest case. Strong counterarguments exist and are worth knowing.

Friends, citizens, defenders of conscience -

There is a question older than our republic, older than democracy itself, and it demands an honest answer from every generation that inherits it:

Who decides which ideas are safe enough for you to hear?

Take a moment with that question. Really sit with it. Because everything - everything - follows from how you answer it.

I. The Foundation

The First Amendment was not written to protect popular speech. Popular speech needs no protection. The majority never needs a shield from itself.

The amendment was written for the heretic. The dissident. The inconvenient prophet. The person who says what powerful people desperately do not want said.

The Founders had just lived through the consequences of a government that decided which political ideas were permissible. They had watched men imprisoned for pamphlets. They had seen sedition laws wielded like clubs against critics of power. They did not build this republic on the naive assumption that future governments would be wiser or kinder. They built it on the hard-won understanding that all governments, including virtuous ones, face the temptation to silence opposition and call the silencing justice.

So they drew a line. A clear, uncompromising line:

Congress shall make no law.

Not: Congress shall make reasonable laws. Not: Congress shall restrict only dangerous speech. Not: Congress shall silence categories we currently agree are harmful.

No law.

II. The Slippery Architecture of Censorship

Now I hear the objection forming in your mind. You're thinking about the exceptions - and you should be. Every argument for censorship begins with an exception so reasonable, so obviously justified, that only a fanatic would refuse it.

"Surely we can prohibit direct incitement to imminent violence?"

Fine. Most free speech advocates accept narrow, tightly defined incitement doctrine.

But notice what happens next. The exception expands. It must expand, because the logic that justified the first exception justifies the second. If we can silence speech that causes physical harm, why not speech that causes psychological harm? If we can silence speech that endangers individuals, why not speech that endangers social stability? If we can silence speech that threatens bodies, why not speech that threatens cherished institutions?

Every authoritarian government in history - every single one - has justified its censorship on precisely these grounds. The Soviet Union criminalized "anti-Soviet agitation." Nazi Germany prohibited "defamation of the Reich." Contemporary authoritarian states outlaw speech that "undermines national unity" or "spreads rumors."

They were not hypocrites. They genuinely believed the speech they suppressed was dangerous. They had experts who testified to the danger. They had public opinion polls showing majorities agreed. They had sincere moral conviction.

Sincerity is not a safeguard. Majorities are not a safeguard. Good intentions are not a safeguard.

The only safeguard is a principle that doesn't bend.

III. The Epistemological Argument

Here is perhaps the deepest reason for free speech protection, and it has nothing to do with law.

We are fallible.

Every generation has held confident moral beliefs that later generations recognized as catastrophic errors. Slavery was defended by the most educated people of their time. The subjugation of women was justified by sophisticated philosophical arguments. The persecution of religious minorities was endorsed by the overwhelming moral consensus of medieval society.

The people who first challenged these consensuses were not celebrated. They were called dangerous. They were called destabilizing. They were called exactly what critics of free speech call unpopular speakers today.

John Stuart Mill understood this. He wrote that even if a prevailing opinion is correct, silencing its opposition produces a harm: the opinion "loses its meaning" and becomes "mere prejudice," "a mere formal profession." We don't just need to hold true beliefs. We need to understand why they are true, so we can defend them, refine them, and recognize when they need revision.

The collision with false ideas is not a bug in the system of open discourse. It is the mechanism by which we find truth.

If you are confident your beliefs are correct, the argument for suppressing opposition is weakest - because truth, as Milton wrote, will "grapple" with falsehood and win. If you are uncertain your beliefs are correct, the argument for suppression is most dangerous - because you may be silencing the correction you need.

IV. The Power Asymmetry Problem

Let me ask you something practical.

When we grant government the power to regulate speech based on content, who exercises that power?

Not philosophers. Not saints. Not a committee of the wisest and most impartial humans alive.

Politicians exercise it. Bureaucrats exercise it. Prosecutors exercise it. People with careers, constituencies, ideological commitments, and personal interests exercise it.

And here is what history teaches us with brutal consistency: speech restrictions are almost never used symmetrically. They are used against the weak, the marginal, the unpopular, the challenging. Labor organizers were prosecuted under early sedition laws. Civil rights leaders were surveilled and harassed under national security frameworks. Anti-war protesters were imprisoned. Suffragists were arrested.

The powerful rarely need speech regulations, because they rarely say things the government wants to suppress. The powerless are the ones silenced.

Every tool of censorship you hand to a government you trust will eventually be inherited by a government you don't. That is not a hypothetical. That is the nature of power transitions in every democracy that has ever existed.

The ACLU - for much of its history, and at its principled best - understood this. That is why it defended Nazis marching in Skokie. Not because Nazism deserves celebration. But because the alternative - giving government the authority to prohibit ideological expression it finds repugnant - creates a precedent that will be turned on civil rights marchers, on labor organizers, on every minority that challenges prevailing power.

You cannot build a censorship machine that only catches the people you hate.

V. The Dignity Argument Reversed

I know the opposing argument. I've heard it made seriously, and I take it seriously.

"Hate speech strips dignity from its targets. Silencing the oppressor protects the oppressed."

This argument comes from a place of genuine moral concern, and I honor that concern.

But consider what it assumes. It assumes that the targets of hateful speech are more damaged by hearing it than by being formally designated by the state as people who require protection from ideas. It assumes that suppression is more empowering than confrontation, refutation, and the development of resilient civic identity. It assumes that the government trusted to define "hate speech" will define it in ways that protect the historically marginalized rather than the currently powerful.

Each of these assumptions is contestable. And the historical record - where "hate speech" frameworks have been used to prosecute civil rights advocates in South Africa, to silence LGBT advocacy in Russia, to criminalize Palestinian solidarity in multiple democracies - should make us deeply suspicious.

The dignity of free citizens is not best protected by shielding them from words. It is protected by trusting them with full civic participation, including the right to hear, evaluate, and publicly refute the worst arguments against their humanity.

VI. What We Ask of Ourselves

I want to be honest with you about what free speech absolutism demands.

It demands that we tolerate speech we find not merely offensive but genuinely harmful in its ideology.

It demands that we trust in the marketplace of ideas even when that market sometimes temporarily elevates bad ideas.

It demands that we bear the discomfort of watching those we despise speak freely, and respond with argument rather than prohibition.

It demands intellectual courage - the willingness to defend a principle even when defending it feels uncomfortable.

These are real costs. Anyone who tells you otherwise is not being straight with you.

But the alternative demands more. It demands that we trust whoever holds power to distinguish redemptive speech from harmful speech, legitimate challenge from dangerous agitation, necessary discomfort from impermissible offense. It demands that we believe the exception we carve out today will not be the template for something far worse tomorrow. It demands that we believe we are wise enough - and that those who come after us will be wise enough - to wield censorship justly.

History does not support that confidence.

VII. The Warning

We stand at a moment when speech restrictions are being proposed - and implemented - across the ideological spectrum. From the right: restricting political content platforms favor, criminalizing protest near certain facilities, suppressing curriculum. From the left: removing speakers from campuses, pressuring platforms to deplatform, criminalizing "disinformation."

Both impulses come from genuine conviction. Both are dangerous.

The principle of free speech is not a partisan instrument. It has no ideology. It protects the civil rights leader and the reactionary, the revolutionary and the defender of tradition, the blasphemer and the devout. That universality is not a flaw. It is the entire point.

The moment free speech becomes conditional - the moment we say "free speech for approved viewpoints" - we have abolished it. We have simply replaced one orthodoxy with another, and handed the next government a ready-made mechanism of suppression pointed at whoever challenges its power.

VIII. Conclusion

So what do I ask of you?

I ask you to resist the seductive comfort of saying: "This speech is so obviously wrong, so clearly harmful, that surely no principle requires us to tolerate it."

That feeling - that certainty - is exactly what every censor in history has felt. It is the emotional signature of the impulse we must discipline.

Instead, I ask you to hold the harder conviction:

That the answer to bad speech is more speech.

That the remedy for dangerous ideas is better ideas, openly argued.

That the protection of liberty requires tolerating its abuse - not because the abuse is acceptable, but because the power to stop it cannot be safely granted to any authority human beings have yet devised.

That free people have the capacity to hear terrible things and respond with reason, evidence, moral argument, and organized civic action.

That the only speech you can be certain deserves protection is the speech that powerful people most want to silence.

Hold that line. Hold it when it's easy and hold it harder when it isn't.

Because the day we decide that liberty is too dangerous for some ideas is the day we begin losing it for all of them.

Thank you.

The strongest counterarguments to this position include: whether "marketplace of ideas" functions equitably across power differentials; whether some speech causes measurable psychological and social harm that warrants different legal treatment; and whether "absolutism" is a coherent position given that all functioning legal systems impose some speech constraints (fraud, perjury, true threats). Engaging these seriously strengthens, rather than weakens, any genuine free speech advocacy.

Hate speech presents the hardest case, precisely because it can demean people and contribute to climates of hostility. But permitting the state to prohibit hateful ideas creates an even broader danger: the government must determine which groups merit protection, what counts as hatred, whether context matters, and which historical or religious claims are forbidden. These decisions are inseparable from politics. Minorities and dissidents may ultimately suffer most, because they often lack the influence needed to shape or resist enforcement. The better answer to hatred is vigorous counterspeech, public condemnation, education, solidarity, and voluntary social consequences—not criminal punishment for expression.

Scientific progress, investigative reporting, and democratic accountability all require room for claims that appear implausible or contradict prevailing authority. Even statements that are plainly false should not become crimes merely because the government declares them so. Officials themselves mislead, conceal information, and make mistakes. Deeply offensive expression must also remain protected. Offense is subjective, culturally variable, and impossible to regulate consistently. Art, satire, blasphemy, protest, and political rhetoric are often intended to shock. A legal right not to be offended would become a veto over everyone else’s freedom. An absolute principle also provides clarity. Once exceptions are created for sufficiently harmful ideas, disputes shift from whether censorship is legitimate to who controls its boundaries. Every faction then seeks to classify its opponents’ speech as uniquely dangerous. A bright-line rule removes that weapon from partisan struggle. It protects everyone equally, regardless of ideology, identity, or influence.

Absolute protection of expression need not mean immunity for separate unlawful conduct. The law may punish violence, trespass, vandalism, fraud, coercion, or harassment directed at particular individuals because those offenses involve conduct or the invasion of concrete rights. Likewise, speech that itself constitutes a transaction—such as entering a contract or ordering an agent to commit a crime—can be treated according to the underlying act. The principle is not that every speaker deserves admiration, but that every citizen must remain beyond the state’s power to dictate permissible thought. Protecting hate speech, misinformation, and offensive content is the price of preventing rulers from defining hatred, truth, and acceptability for everyone.
